summary: Czechia is an EU member state and a member of the Schengen Area. EU citizens can travel there with a valid passport or national ID card. Nationals of the countries on the EU's visa-exempt list (Annex II of Regulation 2018/1806) are exempt from the visa requirement for stays of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period; the ETIAS travel authorisation is not yet in operation. The Czech Foreign Ministry lists the states whose citizens need visas; its standard Schengen visa fee is EUR 90.

tips.text: The UK government tells British travellers that if they are travelling to other Schengen countries as well, their whole visit must be within the 90-day limit, and that visits to Schengen countries in the 180 days before they travel count towards the 90 days.

The Government of Canada says non-official currency exchange is illegal and advises using official exchange offices or banks only. The UK FCDO says Prague city police advise visitors to always change money at a currency exchange or bank rather than on the street, as this money is often counterfeit.

To avoid being overcharged, the Government of Canada advises avoiding hailing taxis on the street and using only officially marked taxis, reputable taxi companies or a trusted ride-sharing app. The UK FCDO says it is safer to use a major taxi company than to pick one up in the street, and to always check the rates on the side of the taxi before getting in.

If you arrive at a Schengen border crossing point for the first time since the EES started, passport control officers will take a photo of your face and/or scan your fingerprints. The EU says this process can be quicker if you register some of your data in advance.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Czechia?
faq.answer: No. The United States is on the EU's list of countries whose nationals are exempt from the visa requirement for stays of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period. ETIAS, the new travel authorisation for visa-exempt travellers with a EUR 20 application fee, is not yet in operation, the EU says.

faq.question: How much does a Czech Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Czech Foreign Ministry gives the Schengen visa fee as EUR 90; children aged 6–11 pay EUR 45 and children up to 6 are free of charge. The visa is for intended stays not exceeding 90 days in any 180-day period. The Visa Code says applications are decided within 15 calendar days, a period that may be extended up to a maximum of 45 calendar days in individual cases.

faq.question: Does Czechia use the euro?
faq.answer: No. The EU says Czechia's currency is the Czech koruna (CZK) and that Czechia is preparing to adopt the euro. The Government of Canada says non-official currency exchange is illegal, and advises never exchanging money with vendors on the street and using official exchange offices or banks only.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Czechia?
faq.answer: Not yet. The EU says ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications are being collected, and that it will announce the start date several months before launch. The ETIAS website lists a EUR 20 application fee.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Czechia without a visa?
faq.answer: Nationals of the countries on the EU's visa-exempt list can stay no more than 90 days in any 180-day period on the territory of the Schengen states; the 180 days preceding each day of stay are considered. EU citizens can travel with a valid passport or national ID card.

As an EU national, you have the right to travel freely in the 27 EU member countries as well as in Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland (non-EU countries but members of the Schengen area) carrying either a valid passport or a national identity card (ID card).

tips.90-180-rule.text: If you’re travelling to other Schengen countries as well, make sure your whole visit is within the 90-day limit. Visits to Schengen countries in the 180 days before you travel count towards your 90 days.

tips.exchange-scams.text: Use official exchange offices or banks only
Prague city police advise visitors to:
always change money at a currency exchange or bank rather than on the street as this money is often counterfeit

tips.taxi-overcharging.text: avoid hailing taxis on the street
use only officially marked taxis, reputable taxi companies or a trusted ride-sharing app
It’s safer to use a major taxi company than to pick one up in the street.
Always check the rates on the side of the taxi before getting in.

entryRequirements.declarations.etias.text: ETIAS is the new travel authorisation for visa-exempt travellers to enter 30 European countries.
These 30 European countries require visa-exempt travellers to have an ETIAS travel authorisation: Austria Belgium Bulgaria Croatia Cyprus Czechia
ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point.
The European Union will inform about the specific date for the start of ETIAS several months prior to its launch.

entryRequirements.customs.currencyLimits.text: If you plan to enter or leave the EU with €10 000 in cash (or its equivalent in other currencies) or carry one or more of the commodities listed below (to the value of €10 000) you must declare it to the customs authorities in the EU country you are entering or leaving, using the EU cash declaration form.

entryRequirements.customs.notes.0.text: If you enter the EU from a non-EU country, you can bring goods free of VAT and excise duties with you if they are not for resale and you respect the limits set out below.
4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer

1 litre of spirits over 22 % vol. (such as vodka or gin) or 1 litre of undenatured alcohol (ethyl alcohol) of 80% vol. (or over) or 2 litres of fortified (for example sherry or port) or sparkling wine
You may carry other goods up to a value of €300 per traveller or €430 for travellers by air and sea.
Depending on the EU country you are visiting, a higher or lower limit may apply.

entryRequirements.customs.notes.1.text: As taxes (VAT and excise) are included in the price of the product in the country where you bought it, no further payments are due in any other EU country.
This exemption applies as long as the products purchased are for your own use and not for resale.
These guideline values may not be lower than the following:
Spirits (for example whiskey or gin) 10 litres
If customs authorities suspect that you are carrying goods which are not for your own use, or are intended for resale, you may be asked to prove that they are (by producing proof of purchase etc.).

countryFacts.safety.text: Petty theft is a problem, especially in major tourist areas in Prague.
Prague city police advise visitors to:
always change money at a currency exchange or bank rather than on the street as this money is often counterfeit
Violent crime is low. Petty crime, such as pickpocketing and purse snatching, is common.

countryFacts.roadVignette.text: The Police of the Czech Republic and Customs Administration of the Czech Republic will perform checks by scanning license plate numbers to see whether the vehicle has a valid electronic vignette or whether it is exempt.
The check is performed on the toll road using patrol cars equipped with cameras to scan the license plates, by connecting to control gates, or by checking at rest stops and parking lots.
A driver found to be on a toll road without a valid electronic vignette (without being exempt) faces a fine of up to CZK 20,000.
